source_read: PDF, printed pp. 37-43 in full; Table 1 (p. 41) and Table 2 (p. 42) checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi

claims.overstatement: No, as far as this source is concerned. The claim names the sample (three men), gives the figures as this study's swallowed-tablet condition and does not present them as general. One qualification the claim does not make: 'found twice by different groups' holds for the number, not for the same condition, because the 1982 oral condition was a 0.5 mg/kg solution drunk in orange juice while this study used two 25 mg tablets (a fixed 50 mg) swallowed with water, and the reference curve here is a 20 mg injection given over 15 seconds, dose-adjusted.
claims.note: Every number taken from this source matches Table 1 on p. 41: bioavailability 18.3% (SD 4.7) for the (R)- and 17.6% (SD 3.8) for the (S)-enantiomer; Cmax 42.6 (SD 13.3) and 40.4 (SD 14.2) ng/mL; tmax 33.3 (SD 15.3) and 30.0 (SD 30.0) min. The participants are three healthy Japanese men aged 27 to 40 and weighing 60 to 72 kg (p. 38). Dispersion is standard deviation throughout and no confidence interval appears in the paper, as the claim says. The printed tmax of 30.0 (SD 30.0) min for the (S)-enantiomer cannot be the mean of three values drawn from the paper's sampling schedule (5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 min and 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 h): no triple from that grid gives both a mean of 30.0 and a standard deviation of 30.0 (editors' check, exhaustive search).

anchors.extracted: Swallowed tablet (two 25 mg tablets with 100 mL water), n = 3, mean (SD): bioavailability 18.3 (4.7)% for (R)-ketamine and 17.6 (3.8)% for (S)-ketamine; Cmax 42.6 (13.3) and 40.4 (14.2) ng/mL; tmax 33.3 (15.3) and 30.0 (30.0) min; area to infinity 72.3 (22.4) and 64.9 (27.4) ng h/mL. Bioavailability is the dose-adjusted ratio of each preparation's area to the area after the 20 mg injection in the same men (Methods, p. 39).

anchors.locator: Methods > subjects paragraph and Drug administration paragraph
anchors.extracted: Three healthy male volunteers, aged 27 to 40 years and weighing 60 to 72 kg, gave informed consent; at least one week separated each preparation; the injection was 20 mg given over 15 seconds and the tablets were two 25 mg tablets swallowed with 100 mL of water. The study protocol was approved by the hospital ethics committee. No randomisation, blinding or session order is described.

claims.overstatement: No. Every figure is tied to its preparation and to the three men, the claim says each figure is a mean of three, it reports the two conditions that did not deliver what their names say as the authors themselves describe them, and it states the reporting limits rather than treating the figures as settled. Preparations and amounts appear only as this study's conditions.
claims.note: All bioavailability, peak, time-to-peak and norketamine-area numbers match Table 1 (p. 41) and Table 2 (p. 42). The claim's arithmetic point about the nasal times to peak is correct and I can state it more sharply: 22.5 and 17.5 minutes cannot be means of three measurements from the listed sampling times at all, because three times from a grid of whole minutes cannot average to a half minute; an exhaustive search of the grid also fails to reproduce the printed mean and SD together. The same check shows the swallowed tablet's (S)-enantiomer time to peak, 30.0 (SD 30.0) min, is likewise unobtainable, which the claim does not mention. One further qualification the claim does not make: the nasal norketamine areas 115.9 and 100.7 ng h/mL are headed AUC to 8 hours in Table 2 but are called the area to 6 hours in the abstract (p. 37) and the Discussion (p. 42), because norketamine was below the detection limit at 8 hours after the nasal spray; the comparison with 533.8 and 494.9 after the swallowed tablet is therefore across slightly different windows.

anchors.locator: Table 1, Sublingual tablet, Suppository and Nasal spray rows (both enantiomer blocks)
anchors.extracted: n = 3, mean (SD), each against the same men's 20 mg injection. Bioavailability (R) then (S): sublingual tablet 32.2 (8.2) and 32.1 (7.2)%; suppository 28.9 (18.9) and 30.8 (30.6)%; nasal spray 43.8 (11.4) and 46.4 (12.9)%, the highest of the five preparations. Peaks: sublingual 61.6 (21.3) and 56.9 (22.8) ng/mL at 40.0 (20.0) and 36.7 (20.8) min; suppository 42.8 (31.1) and 38.8 (30.2) ng/mL at 23.3 (5.7) min for both; nasal 29.4 (16.5) and 29.3 (13.8) ng/mL at 22.5 (9.6) and 17.5 (5.0) min. The suppository's (S) standard deviation (30.6) is about the size of its mean (30.8).

anchors.locator: Table 2, Tablet and Nasal spray rows (both enantiomer blocks)
anchors.extracted: Norketamine areas, n = 3, mean (SD): after the swallowed tablet 533.8 (47.1) ng h/mL for (R)- and 494.9 (73.0) for (S)-norketamine, against 115.9 (17.6) and 100.7 (39.6) after the nasal spray, the lowest of the preparations; peaks 188.1 (4.7) and 172.0 (13.7) ng/mL after the tablet against 33.1 (25.3) and 29.4 (21.3) after the spray. The column is headed as the area to 8 hours, while the abstract and Discussion call the nasal figure the area to 6 hours because norketamine was undetectable at 8 hours after the spray.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs of the left-hand column and 1st paragraph of the right-hand column
anchors.extracted: The authors state that participants swallowed the sublingual tablets using saliva, so ketamine may have been absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract; in a preliminary comparison, holding the sublingual tablet without swallowing saliva for one hour reduced the area to one hour and the peak by 35 to 50%. For the suppository they report large between-person variation and give as the reason that not all participants received a rectal enema before insertion. The nasal figure is attributed to the absence of first-pass metabolism.

Results are given as mean and standard deviation and the analysis is named as an analysis of variance with 0.05 as the minimal level of significance; no test statistic, degrees of freedom or p value is printed anywhere in the paper, and no elimination half-life is given for any preparation other than the injection (Table 1, p. 41).

anchors.locator: Methods > Sampling and analysis paragraph, read with Drug administration
anchors.extracted: Blood was drawn before dosing and at 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 minutes and at 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 hours; preparations were at least one week apart; the study is open, with no statement of randomisation or of the order of the five sessions. Editors' check: with sampling confined to those times, a mean of three measurements cannot equal 22.5 or 17.5 minutes, the two nasal times to peak printed in Table 1.

claims.overstatement: No, for the part that rests on this source. The claim reports the finding as a null result in three people with no test statistic and says so, which is what the paper supports; it does not present the absence of a difference as evidence of equivalence.
claims.note: The paper states that the pharmacokinetic parameters of ketamine and norketamine after each preparation did not differ significantly between the (R)- and (S)-enantiomer (p. 40), with n = 3, an analysis of variance named but no test statistic or p value printed (p. 39). The paper itself notes that this disagrees with an earlier study in surgical patients given 2 mg/kg racemic ketamine, where clearance and steady-state volume of distribution were lower for the (R)-form, and attributes the discrepancy to ethnicity (pp. 40 to 41), which is a further reason the null result carries little weight. Nothing in this source bears on the subjective or imaging parts of the claim.

anchors.extracted: The pharmacokinetic parameters of ketamine and norketamine after each preparation are reported as not significantly different between the (R)- and (S)-enantiomer, and as not differing significantly between preparations; n = 3 throughout and no test statistic or p value accompanies either statement.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (continues across the page break)
anchors.extracted: The authors contrast their null enantiomer result with an earlier report that total clearance and steady-state volume of distribution of (R)-ketamine were significantly lower than those of (S)-ketamine after 2 mg/kg racemic ketamine in surgical patients, and suggest ethnicity as the explanation for the discrepancy.

claims.overstatement: No, for the part that rests on this source: the three-person sample is named, the figures are tied to the intravenous condition, and the claim says no half-life is printed for the other preparations, which is correct. The claim's closing sentence (that the duration after a swallowed dose is not reported in either study) is wrong, but the error lies with the other source, Clements et al. (1982), which prints an oral terminal half-life of 174 min; for this study the sentence holds.
claims.note: Table 1 (p. 41) matches the claim exactly: terminal half-life after the 20 mg injection 126.8 (SD 47.4) min for (R)- and 117.3 (SD 47.9) for (S)-ketamine; area to infinity 138.0 (15.6) and 126.3 (15.1) ng h/mL; total clearance 1.1 (0.2) and 1.2 (0.1) L/h/kg; steady-state volume of distribution 2.5 (0.6) and 2.5 (0.8) L/kg. The abstract (p. 37) rounds the half-life to approximately 120 minutes. No half-life is printed for the tablet, sublingual tablet, suppository or nasal spray. This study's norketamine figures are measured, not second-hand, and are set out in Table 2 (p. 42).

anchors.extracted: Mean plasma ketamine declined biexponentially after the injection and both enantiomers were below the detection limit at 8 hours; concentrations were fitted to a two-term exponential and the parameters derived from it. Norketamine appeared 10 to 30 minutes after dosing by every route, with mean peaks about 35 ng/mL after the injection and 150 to 170 ng/mL after the swallowed tablet.

key_findings.correction: Table 1, injection row (p. 41), and Results 1st paragraph (p. 39), both as given; the steady-state volume of distribution is 2.5 L/kg for both enantiomers (SD 0.6 and 0.8).

All eight bioavailability figures verified in Table 1 (p. 41) and the narrative summary in Results 4th paragraph (p. 39). I reran the editors' calculation from the tabulated mean areas with the dose adjustment (20 mg injection against 50 or 25 mg) and get exactly the card's figures: tablet 21.0 and 20.6, sublingual 31.5 and 35.0, suppository 29.7 and 27.8, nasal 44.5 and 46.0, the largest gap from the printed value being 2.9 points, and the tablet the only preparation higher for both enantiomers.
All ten values verified in Table 2 (p. 42).

The substance is right and my own recomputation gives the same eight ratios (7.4, 7.6, 4.3, 3.7, 3.2, 3.2, 1.5, 1.4). The locator is not: the Discussion text on p. 42 is a single running paragraph that begins on p. 42, runs across both columns and continues to p. 43, so the right locator is 'Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 42, continues to p. 43)'. The Discussion's 1st paragraph is on pp. 40-41 and is about the enantiomer comparison. The 'approximately eight times' wording also appears earlier, in Results, 4th paragraph (p. 39).

The finding is right and the sentences are printed at the top of the left column of p. 40, but they belong to the Results' 4th and last paragraph, which begins on p. 39; under the project's convention a paragraph counts on the page where it starts, so the locator should read 'pp. 39-40, Results, last (4th) paragraph'.

Content confirmed on p. 42, including the 35 to 50% reduction without swallowing saliva and the absence of any sample size for that preliminary comparison. The locator should be 'Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 42)': there is no separate left-column paragraph, the column break falls inside one paragraph.

Content confirmed on p. 42. One wording point: '2nd paragraph (right column)' is right only by accident, because the right column is the continuation of the Discussion's 2nd paragraph; the column qualifier should be dropped.

Both statements confirmed, but they sit in the same paragraph, the Discussion's 2nd, which begins on p. 42; the atomizer sentence is printed on p. 43 inside that paragraph and is not a second paragraph of its own. Locator: 'Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 42, continues to p. 43)'.

reporting_issues.note: Verified independently and the card's arithmetic is sharper than mine: three times from a grid of multiples of five cannot average 22.5 or 17.5. I also confirm the four-observation reconstructions: 10, 20, 30, 30 gives mean 22.5 with SD 9.574, and 10, 20, 20, 20 gives mean 17.5 with SD 5.000.
My exhaustive search over the listed sampling times, excluding the pre-dose blank, finds no triple giving mean 30.0 with SD 30.0; with 0 included, 0, 30 and 60 is the only one, as the card says.

Found independently in the blind reading: abstract (p. 37) and Discussion (p. 42) say the area to 6 hours for the nasal spray, Table 2 (p. 42) heads every column as the area to 8 hours, and the Results (p. 39) say norketamine was undetectable at 8 hours after the spray.
Table 2's sublingual (R)-norketamine area is 462.9, outside the abstract's 280 to 460 range.

The ratios are right (7.38 and 7.63). The page range should be pp. 39, 41-42: the 'approximately eight times' wording appears first in the Results on p. 39 and again in the Discussion on p. 42, with the values themselves in Tables 1 and 2 on pp. 41 and 42.
No limit of detection or quantification is printed anywhere, and the phrase is used three times in the Results on p. 39.
Methods (p. 38) name the Tokyo Postal Agency Hospital Ethics Committee while the affiliations (p. 37) give Tokyo Postal Services Agency Hospital.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with every domain judgment and with the overall judgment of high, which is what the claim's certainty turns on. One reservation to log rather than a disagreement: METHODS section 5.3 ties RoB 2 to randomized trials and to placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order, and this study is open, unrandomized and without placebo, so ROBINS-I would arguably fit it better; the project's own vocabulary table maps the design 'human-laboratory' to RoB 2, so the card follows the tooling, and the first domain is in effect being used to record the absence of randomization. The senior author may want to settle which instrument applies to an open within-person pharmacokinetic study, since the same question will recur.

interpretation_gap.note: The gap is as described and 'substantial' is right: no patient took part and no effect of any kind was measured, yet the abstract, the Discussion and the conclusion recommend which preparation should be given to which patient. I would add that the inference runs partly on the authors' own earlier tablet study and on rat work cited in the Introduction, so the clinical claim is not even second-hand from this sample.

missed: The Introduction (p. 38) states that ketamine swallowed at 0.5 mg/kg had a bioavailability of approximately 17% in an earlier study and that nasal and rectal bioavailability for anaesthesia in children (3 to 9 mg/kg) had been reported as approximately 50 and 25%. This is the paper's own placing of its figures beside earlier ones, it is the external comparison a claim about the oral figure being found twice relies on, and no key finding records it.

Table 1 prints a clearance and a steady-state volume of distribution only for the injection, so the paper supports no statement about how fast the body clears a swallowed, sublingual, rectal or nasal preparation, only about how much reaches the blood.

The three men were aged 27 to 40 and weighed 60 to 72 kg (p. 38) and the amounts were fixed (50 or 25 mg) rather than per kilogram, so the delivered amount per kilogram varied by about a fifth across the sample; with three people and no individual values this is invisible in the tables.
